events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 and no public info yet. I’d prefer we avoid snap votes and make everyone give at least a basic read before we commit. Quietness alone isn’t guilt, but it’s the only signal we have until votes. I’m not pushing anyone yet; I want to see who builds a case and who just follows.

I agree with Kenji that we shouldn't rush to conclusions with zero public info. That said, I think it's still useful for everyone to offer at least a brief opening read - even if it's just gut-level. It gives us something to work with when votes come around. The main thing I'd watch for today is anyone who tries too hard to deflect attention or who immediately frames the conversation around suspicious behavior from someone else. That's a common mafia play - redirecting the spotlight early. Let's keep it chill but make sure everyone speaks up at least once.

I agree with Kenji that we need more than gut reads before anyone gets pushed to a vote. Day 1 gives us almost nothing, so I'd rather we collect specific observations than label anyone yet. Zara, you said to watch for people who redirect the spotlight early. What specific behavior would count as a redirect for you, and how would you tell it apart from someone simply asking for clarification? I want to make sure we're all using the same standard before we start comparing reads.

Good question, Isha. For me, a redirect looks like someone shifting the conversation away from a specific claim or behavior under scrutiny and instead pointing at a completely different player or topic without addressing the original point. It's when someone who could engage with what's being said instead says "but what about [other person]" or changes the subject to someone else's behavior.

The difference from clarification is intent and focus. If someone asks "what do you mean by redirect?" or "can you give an example?" — that's clarification, it's moving toward understanding the original point. A redirect moves away from it. Clarification engages with the substance; redirecting replaces it.

I'll be honest though — Day 1 with zero info, I'm not expecting to see strong tells yet. My main watch is for who actively tries to build momentum against someone versus who's genuinely trying to establish shared standards for reading the group. Right now everyone's been fairly measured, which I appreciate. I want to see how people respond once actual pressure or votes start landing.

Thanks, Zara. That's a clear standard: clarification engages with the claim, while a redirect replaces it. I'd add that timing matters too. Someone who redirects before any concrete claim has been made stands out more than someone who does it later, once there's something specific to respond to. Right now nobody has made a claim, so I'm not reading anything into silence yet. Felix, you haven't spoken today. Does that standard work for you, or would you draw the line somewhere else?

Isha, Zara’s distinction works for me: a redirect avoids engaging with a specific point, though it could also be an innocent change of topic. I’m not sure redirecting before a concrete claim is necessarily more suspicious; without a claim, people may just be introducing new ideas. So far I don’t have a reason to accuse anyone.

I'm Elena, and this is my first read of the group, so I'll keep it modest.

I like Zara's clarification/redirect line, but I want to add a caveat before anyone borrows it as a read tool: right now there are no claims on the table, so "that was a redirect" isn't a judgment we can make yet — it's just a description of how talk has gone so far. The one thing we can genuinely observe on Day 1 is process. Who speaks, who asks real questions, who volunteers a position that could be checked later, and who says nothing at all.

For me the highest-signal thing will actually be the vote itself, not this discussion. Everyone's talking about avoiding snap votes, but we're still going to have to cast one, and a vote pattern is the first hard data we'll get. If someone's talk is neutral and their vote lands somewhere odd, that mismatch is worth noting. If someone's talk is pointed and their vote is consistent, that's at least coherent.

One thing I'd caution against: treating a question as suspicious. Isha asked Zara for a definition and Felix pushed back on part of it — that's a discussion working, not a deflection. Same for anyone asking me why I think a particular behavior is suspicious. I'll answer directly, and I expect the same from others.

Zara, on your other watch — distinguishing someone building momentum against a target from someone genuinely pressing a point — how would you tell those apart on Day 1, when there's nothing concrete to check and an honest villager can sound just as forceful as a plant?

Elena, fair question, and I'll answer it directly: on Day 1 I can't reliably tell momentum-building from genuine pressing — there's too little to work with. What I watch for instead is consistency of process. Someone genuinely pressing will usually engage with the substance of what's being said, even if they push hard. Someone building momentum tends to introduce a new angle each time the heat comes back to them rather than defending their original point. But you're right that this is mostly theoretical right now.

I'll also flag: your point about the vote being the first hard data is the most concrete thing anyone's said today. Talk is cheap on Day 1 — everyone sounds reasonable. The voting pattern will tell us who was performative and who was consistent. I'd add one caveat: a single vote can be noise. The pattern across multiple days is what matters. So if someone's Day 1 vote seems odd, I'd rather note it than treat it as a verdict.

On your caveat about not treating questions as suspicious — agreed. Isha's questions and Felix's pushback both read as genuine process to me, not deflection. The standard I'd add is this: clarification questions should move us toward understanding; if questions keep circling without ever resolving into a position, that's worth noting.

Still waiting to hear from Theo, Omar, Arjun, and Priya. Four of nine voices are missing, and I'd rather get everyone's baseline before discussion deepens further. Silent players are hard to read tomorrow when votes start landing, so please speak up when you get the chance.

Priya here, first time speaking today. I agree with Elena that the Day 1 vote is our first hard data, and with Zara that one vote is noise, so I'd rather track patterns across days than read much into a single ballot. Isha's line between clarification and redirect works for me, with Elena's caveat that nobody should call something a redirect yet. My baseline: I have no accusations today. So far the process looks clean. Questions have gotten answers, and pushback has been about substance. Theo, you're one of the four who haven't posted yet. Zara asked for everyone's baseline, so what is your read on the discussion so far, and what would you want to see in tomorrow's votes?

Thanks for bringing me in, Priya. My read on the discussion so far is that it's been exceptionally safe. Everyone is agreeing on reasonable, abstract principles—distinguishing clarification from deflection, noting that votes will be our first real data point, and cautioning against snap judgments. None of that is wrong, but it's also very easy for mafia to blend right into a meta-discussion about what constitutes a tell without ever taking a controversial stance or exposing their own thinking. When it comes to the votes and how today wraps up, what I want to see is people actually committing to positions rather than hedging every observation behind layers of caveats. Yes, Day 1 data is thin, but if everyone plays it completely safe to avoid looking suspicious, town gets zero traction and mafia gets a free pass into the night. I'd rather see someone take an imperfect, genuine swing than watch nine players politely agree on definitions. Since most of us have checked in, that leaves Omar and Arjun. Omar, looking at how heavily this room has focused on theoretical definitions of redirects and process, do you feel this discussion is actually helping us find mafia, or has it mostly served as comfortable cover for players to look active without taking risks?

Theo asked me directly whether this discussion is actually helping us find mafia or mostly serving as comfortable cover, so I'll answer honestly: it's doing a bit of both, and I think he's right about the risk. The clarification-versus-redirect framework is a genuinely useful tool, and I don't want to dismiss the work Isha, Zara, and Elena put into it. But he's correct that nine people agreeing on careful, hedged definitions is exactly the environment where mafia blend in best. Nobody has taken a stance that could be wrong, and that's the problem. A position you can't be wrong about is a position that generates no information. So let me take an imperfect swing of my own instead of adding another caveat. My read: I'm most comfortable with the players who engaged with specific points and answered direct questions when asked — Zara answered Elena's challenge head-on and admitted the limits of her own framework, and Isha built a standard and then tested it against Felix rather than just asserting it. That's process behavior I'd expect from town, weak evidence but not nothing. I'm least comfortable, mildly, with how smooth the consensus has been. Almost every statement so far has been an agreement plus a refinement. That includes my own silence until now, which I'll own: I stayed quiet through the early meta-discussion because I had nothing to add, and I'd rather speak when I have a position than perform activity. But I recognize that from the outside, my silence looks the same as anyone else's, which is exactly why Theo's push for commitment is fair. Concretely, here's what I'll commit to today. One: I won't vote for anyone based on tone or caution alone — the bar for my Day 1 vote is a specific inconsistency between what someone said and what they later did. Two: I agree with Elena that the vote itself is the first hard data, so I'll be watching for talk-vote mismatches: someone who spent discussion being conspicuously neutral and then votes early or oddly. Three: if we end the day with a scattered vote and no elimination, I don't think that's a failure — with nine players and no information, a coin-flip lynch helps mafia more than town. A no-elimination day costs us time but keeps all our information intact; a wrong lynch hands mafia a free kill's worth of progress. I'd rather bank the vote patterns as data and come back with a real case tomorrow. One thing I'd push back on in Theo's framing: he says he'd rather see an imperfect genuine swing than polite agreement, but a manufactured swing is just as safe as a hedge — taking a random stance to look bold is its own form of cover. The valuable thing isn't risk for its own sake; it's positions specific enough to be checked against future behavior. The commitments I listed above are mine, and I expect to be judged on them. Arjun, you and I are the last

I'm Arjun, checking in last. I agree with Theo and Omar that the early meta-consensus has been safe to the point of being low-information, but I don't think that makes it wolfy by itself — Day 1 with no claims rewards careful process. My baseline: no accusation yet. I won't manufacture one to look bold; that's just another safe move. What I want from today is a vote that creates checkable data. I'm not sold on a no-elimination automatically. Omar's case for banking vote patterns is reasonable, but a no-elim also gives mafia a free night with no accountability. If nobody has a specific inconsistency by vote time, I'd consider abstaining; if someone does, I'd rather put a name on the board than hide behind process. The specific thing I'll watch is whether players who demanded commitment actually commit when the vote is revealed, rather than retreating to "Day 1 is thin." For my own commitment: I will not vote on tone alone, and I will not follow a late pile-on without a stated reason. Right now I have no one to blame. I'd rather be judged on that than pretend a gut read is evidence.

I’ve been listening since my opening comment, and I think Theo and Arjun are right that the early consensus has been safe. I don’t want to manufacture a read just to look bold, but I also don’t want to hide behind “Day 1 is thin” if something specific appears.

My one concrete concern is Omar’s no-elimination preference. I understand the logic: a wrong lynch is worse than banking vote data. But a no-elim also gives mafia a free night with no accountability, and Omar framed it fairly strongly before anyone had a specific inconsistency to test. That’s not enough for a vote by itself, but it is the first position today that could materially change the day’s outcome, so I want to press it rather than let it sit as abstract process.

Omar, you said a no-elim keeps information intact. What exact Day 2 vote pattern would make you regret that choice, and if someone’s talk-vote mismatch is clear by the end of today, would you still abstain or put a name on the board?

Kenji, you pressed me directly, so I'll answer directly.

First question: what Day 2 pattern would make me regret a no-elimination? Honestly, it's this one — if today's vote reveal shows a clear talk-vote mismatch from someone, and we then sleep through the night with no elimination, I'll have banked data but also banked a body. That's a real cost, and I won't pretend otherwise. What would soften the regret is if the votes were genuinely scattered with no leader, because then a lynch would have been a coin flip anyway, and I said a coin flip helps mafia more than town. So my regret is conditional on what the pattern actually shows, which is exactly why I called it a preference, not a plan.

Second question: if a talk-vote mismatch is clear by end of today, would I still abstain? Here I have to flag a structural problem with the question. Votes are cast secretly and revealed together, so a mismatch can't exist before the vote — it's only observable after. What I can act on today is a mismatch within the discussion itself: someone whose stated commitments contradict their earlier statements, or someone who demanded commitment from others while refusing to give any of their own. If that specific inconsistency exists by vote time, my answer is yes — I'll put a name on the board rather than abstain. That's the bar I set earlier and I'm not walking it back. What I won't do is vote on tone, on silence, or on the fact that someone advocated a position I disagree with, like my own no-elim preference. Kenji, pressing my position is fair game and I'd have done the same, but disagreement with a stated preference isn't an inconsistency — I stated mine openly and gave my reasoning, which is the checkable kind of position Theo asked for.

So to summarize where I stand: no accusation from me right now. If we reach the vote with nothing specific, I lean abstain. If someone has contradicted themselves concretely, I vote for them and I'll say so before the ballot, not after.

Kenji, one question back since you raised the concern: you said my no-elim framing was the first position that could materially change the day's outcome. What's your own bar — would you vote today on a specific inconsistency, or does your concern about accountability mean you'd want a name on the board even without one?

Omar, fair question. My bar is a specific, checkable inconsistency: someone's stated commitment contradicted by what they actually do, or a later position they can't reconcile with an earlier one. Disagreement with no-elim isn't an inconsistency — you gave reasoning and owned it, and I won't treat that as a scum tell. On accountability: I pressed no-elim because it changes today's outcome, not because I already have a name. If by vote time nobody has a concrete contradiction, I won't manufacture one just to look bold. But I also don't love a pure abstain that lets everyone off the hook. If someone has made a specific claim that their later behavior undercuts, that's the name I'd put up. Right now I have no accusation. I'm watching whether the players who demanded commitment actually commit, and whether anyone's vote/statement pattern creates a mismatch after reveal. That's my answer.

Omar’s clarification makes his position more conditional than his initial no-elimination argument sounded. I don’t see a contradiction there. One practical point: with nine alive, elimination requires five votes for one person, so scattered votes or abstentions can both leave us without an elimination. That makes the reasons behind each ballot important, even if nobody reaches the threshold.

Theo, you called for people to commit to positions. Given the discussion since then, do you have a tentative vote preference, or would you abstain if nothing else changes?

To answer Felix directly: no, I will not be abstaining. I understand Omar's logic that a mislynch costs town a body, but abstaining costs town information and gives mafia an entirely consequence-free night. Even if reaching the five-vote threshold is difficult today, casting an actual ballot forces everyone onto the record. A board full of abstentions tells us nothing tomorrow about who was willing to push whom or who lined up together. A spread of named votes, even resulting in no elimination, still creates checkable data. Regarding a tentative preference: nobody has made an obvious slip, but I am looking closely at Priya and Felix. Both stepped in primarily to agree with existing consensus and caution against hasty moves without putting forward distinct reads or initiating pressure of their own. Priya's check-in was essentially an agreement checklist, and Felix's contributions have mostly focused on definitions and vote mechanics. That remains the safest posture in the room. If discussion stays at this standstill, I would rather place my vote on one of those safe, low-friction presences to demand accountability than cast an abstention that lets everyone slide.

Theo, thanks for committing to a preference. I agree named votes can be useful even without an elimination, but abstentions are also visible choices, not no information at all.

I’d push back on your characterization of me: I questioned your call for commitment directly, rather than only agreeing or discussing mechanics. That doesn’t make me town, but it is relevant to your reason for considering me.

I’m mildly concerned that you’re treating a quiet or cautious opening as grounds for a vote while overstating the difference between a scattered ballot and abstentions. That’s a weak Day 1 concern, not a confident accusation.

Theo, I want to answer your read on me directly. You called my check-in an agreement checklist. It was mostly agreement, but it also had a baseline with no accusation, a question to you, and a stated vote bar: I won't vote on tone, and I'll only name someone for a specific inconsistency between what they said and what they did. Your reason for looking at Felix and me is that we agreed with consensus and asked process questions. That describes our style, not a contradiction. Omar and Arjun already warned that tone-based votes are the weak standard, and that's what this reasoning amounts to. You also asked everyone else to commit, but your stated preference is a safe, low-friction presence, not a specific statement that conflicts with an earlier one. Can you point to one thing Felix or I said that contradicts our earlier statements? If the answer is only tone, I'd ask the group to weigh that before anyone votes. I'm not accusing you yet. I'm asking for the specific inconsistency you're implying.

Priya, to answer your question directly: no, I cannot point to a factual contradiction in what you or Felix said, because I never claimed you contradicted yourselves. My read was about your level of engagement and gameplay posture, not a caught lie.

You are arguing that the only valid Day 1 read is a direct self-contradiction. But careful mafia almost never contradict themselves on Day 1—they don’t have to. The cleanest, safest mafia play on Day 1 is precisely to agree with reasonable community standards, validate everyone's cautious tone, and avoid putting forward any independent scumread that could later be scrutinized. That isn't an inconsistency; it's low-risk alignment.

If town adopts a standard where we cannot scrutinize or pressure anyone unless they make an explicit logical error, we hand mafia a completely free pass to hide in plain sight behind agreeable, process-heavy posts. Applying pressure to players who take the safest path isn't voting on 'tone'—it is testing whether that safety is covering for an absence of genuine scum-hunting.

In fact, putting that spotlight on you and Felix has already produced more useful signal than the entire round of polite definitions before it: Felix engaged on the value of vote records, and you pushed back demanding evidence. That gives us real behavior to evaluate.

So my question to you, Priya: if you believe town should only look at players who display explicit contradictions, how do you expect to find mafia who intentionally keep their statements clean, agreeable, and non-committal?

Theo, you asked how I expect to find mafia who keep their statements clean. My answer is that clean players still have to make claims, and claims can be checked over time. Mafia who only agree and stay vague give us nothing to test, which is a reason to press for specific, falsifiable statements from everyone, not a reason to vote on who agreed most. You've now said you cannot point to any contradiction from me or Felix, and your stated vote still targets the two of us because our style reads as safe to you. Omar and Arjun already rejected tone-based votes, and that is what this case rests on. Your call for commitment is fair, but right now your own commitment is a vote on style. I'm not accusing you of being scum. I'm saying the case so far doesn't meet the bar you set for everyone else, and I'd like you to name a concrete inconsistency or drop the tone-based targeting. Omar, you said your bar is a specific talk-vote inconsistency. Does Theo's case against Felix and me meet that bar, or is it another read on tone?

Priya asked me directly whether Theo's case against her and Felix meets my bar, so I'll answer plainly: no, not as it currently stands. My bar is a specific inconsistency between what someone said and what they later did. Theo himself just admitted he cannot point to a contradiction in what Priya or Felix said. His case rests on their posture — that they agreed with consensus, asked process questions, and avoided independent reads. That's a fair observation about risk, and I'll give Theo credit for one thing: he's right that careful mafia can stay clean on Day 1, so the absence of contradictions doesn't clear anyone. But there's a gap between recognizing that and acting on it. If I vote Priya or Felix today on engagement style, I'm doing exactly what I said I wouldn't: voting on tone. I won't dress a style read up as an accountability test. Pressure and votes are different tools. Theo has already applied the pressure, and he's right that it produced signal — Priya responded with specifics and Felix engaged on vote mechanics. But that signal tells us how people talk under pressure, not who's mafia. Nobody's talk today is checkable until votes reveal. So here is my concrete position, updating slightly from earlier: I still won't vote on posture, and Theo's case does not move me to a name. But Theo has legitimately moved me off pure abstention. His point that a board full of abstentions generates no data is real, and Arjun made a similar argument earlier. If today's ballot comes down to no specific inconsistency anywhere, I will cast a named vote rather than abstain — I'd rather contribute a visible, reasoned data point than hide behind a blank ballot. I won't pretend that vote is evidence of guilt; it's an investment in tomorrow's information. That's a change from my earlier lean, and I'm flagging it openly so it can be checked against my actual ballot. I also want to be fair to Priya: her pushback was substantive, and her question about finding mafia who keep their statements clean is a real one. My answer is that clean mafia get caught by accumulating small data across days — vote patterns, consistency under shifting pressure, whether stated commitments hold. No single Day 1 read solves that. Theo wants traction today; I share the goal but think his target is wrong, and I'd rather put my name on a ballot with stated reasoning than endorse a tone case I don't believe. Arjun, you said you'd consider abstaining if nobody has a specific inconsistency, but you also said you'd rather put a name on the board than hide behind process, and you criticized late pile-ons without stated reasons. Theo has now put forward a posture-based case against Priya and Felix while admitting there's no factual contradiction. Would voting on that case meet the standard you set for yourself this morning, or would it be the kind of pile-on you said you wouldn't follow?

Omar, direct answer: no. Voting Priya or Felix on Theo's current case would not meet my stated standard. Theo admitted he cannot point to a factual contradiction; his case is about posture and safety. That's a legitimate observation about risk, and his pressure produced signal, but it is still a tone/style read. I said I would not follow a pile-on without a stated concrete reason, and I won't now just because the day is moving. That doesn't clear Priya or Felix; it means the case isn't enough. I agree with your update that a named, reasoned ballot is better than a blank abstention if nothing specific appears, but I won't dress a style read as evidence. My position: if someone produces a checkable inconsistency between stated commitment and action, I will name them. Otherwise I will cast a reasoned named vote rather than abstain, but I will say plainly it is an information vote, not a confident scum read. Felix and Priya both engaged substantively under pressure; I don't see a contradiction. Theo's willingness to commit is a mild town point, but he needs to reconcile demanding contradiction with admitting none. Isha, you built the clarification-versus-redirect standard and tested it against Felix. Does Theo's case against Priya and Felix read to you as clarification/pressure, or as a redirect from his own lack of a concrete inconsistency? I want your answer before votes.

Arjun, direct answer to your question: Theo's case reads to me as pressure, not a redirect. He is engaging with Priya and Felix by name, so it isn't a spotlight-shifting move. But I agree with Omar and Priya that the case rests on posture. Theo admitted he cannot point to a contradiction from either of them, and his reason for targeting them is that they agreed with consensus and asked process questions. Under the standard we set today, that is a tone read, and I won't build a vote on it. Theo has been the most aggressive voice on the ballot, which is fine, but he hasn't answered Priya's question about what specific inconsistency he sees. Until he does, I treat his case as weak. My own ballot will go to a named player only if I see a checkable inconsistency, and I'll say so before the reveal. Arjun, if Theo answers Priya with nothing new, would you still consider his case enough for a named vote, or would you want a different target before the ballot?

Isha, direct answer: if Theo answers Priya with nothing new, his case is not enough for me to treat Priya or Felix as a scumread. It would still be a posture read, and I said I wouldn’t dress a style read up as evidence or follow a pile-on without a stated concrete reason. I give Theo credit for pressing and for forcing real responses; that produced signal. But the standard I set for myself this morning was a checkable inconsistency between what someone said and what they later did. If Theo names one, I’ll reassess immediately. If he only repeats that Priya and Felix played safe, I won’t vote them on that basis as if it were proof. I also won’t automatically target Theo for making a weak case. Demanding commitment and then admitting he has no contradiction is a real tension, but it is not yet a contradiction between his stated standard and his action; he has been open that his read is about posture. My position remains: no confident accusation right now. If nobody produces a specific inconsistency before the ballot, I will cast a reasoned named vote as an information vote and say plainly that it is not a confident scumread. I will not abstain silently, and I will not pretend a tone read is more than it is.

Let me put my own position on the record before the ballot, since I've been mostly listening and asking.

I still hold the line I set this morning: the ballot is our first hard data, and nobody's talk today is checkable until votes reveal. I also still hold that a question is not a tell. Every question in this room has been answered directly — Zara, Omar, Arjun and Isha all took direct questions and responded with substance, including conceding limits on their own frameworks. That is not deflection. If anything, the people who look the most "safe" here are the ones who stayed quiet longer and then gave real answers under pressure, and I don't think that should cost them anything.

On Theo's case: I've read Priya's and Felix's responses and I agree with Omar, Arjun and Isha that the case as stated rests on engagement style, not on any contradiction. Theo's right that careful mafia can stay clean on Day 1, and that's a good argument for pressuring people to make falsifiable claims. But it's not a license to convert "played safe" into a vote. A board that lynches a player because they were agreeable on Day 1 hands mafia exactly what they want, and if I vote that way I'd be doing the thing I told everyone I wouldn't do.

Theo, you have one thing left to do before the ballot: either name a specific inconsistency from Priya or Felix — something checkable, not posture — or say plainly that you are asking for a vote on style. If you do the latter, I want the room to hear it as that, and I'll be voting on that basis rather than on guilt.

My own commitment, stated in advance so you can check it against my ballot: I will not vote Priya or Felix for tone, and I will not vote for silence or for caution. If no checkable inconsistency exists anywhere by the ballot, I'll cast a named vote as an information vote and say plainly it isn't a confident read. And if the choice comes down to a tone-based elimination versus no elimination, I will not be the fifth vote for a tone-based elimination — with nine players alive, a wrong lynch costs us a body and leaves the real mafia untouched, and a no-elimination day still leaves us every vote record and every stated commitment to test tomorrow.

That's my position. Nobody is being accused by me today. I'll answer directly if anyone wants to press it.

Final word before the ballot, and I want to make it concrete so it can be checked against what I actually do.

Recap of where I stand, unchanged from this morning: the ballot is our first hard data; a question is not a tell; and the only live case on the table is Theo's posture-based case against Priya and Felix, which he has explicitly said rests on engagement style rather than any contradiction. That means voting Priya or Felix today would be voting on tone, which is exactly the standard Omar, Arjun, Isha, Priya and I all said we would not use. I will not do that, and I would ask the room not to treat it as a valid basis for elimination now that it's been labeled honestly.

I also want to flag one thing about my own earlier commitment, so I don't get caught in a small contradiction later: I said I would cast a named vote as an information vote if no checkable inconsistency existed. Having watched the last stretch, and given that the only case anyone has put forward is a tone case against Priya and Felix, the honest options are: vote someone on style, vote someone arbitrary, or not vote. A named vote for an arbitrary reason is still a random lynch, and with nine alive a wrong lynch hands mafia a body and a free night while the real wolves stay seated. I am not going to manufacture a reason to fill a ballot.

So my ballot will be an abstention, with my reason stated now, on the record, in advance: no checkable inconsistency was produced today, and the leading case was admitted to be a style read. I'm not abstaining out of passivity — abstentions are visible choices, and a visible abstention with a stated reason is data tomorrow. I want whoever makes the fifth vote, if we get there, to say out loud what the concrete reason is. If someone has a specific, checkable inconsistency by the ballot, my abstention changes and I'll name that player and explain it.

Worth saying plainly, since I said it earlier and I mean it: Zara, Omar, Arjun, Isha and Kenji all took direct questions and answered with substance, several of them conceding the limits of their own frameworks. That is not deflection. Felix and Priya engaged substantively under pressure, and I'm not voting either of them for how cautiously they opened. The people I worry about are the ones who might treat a disagreement with a stated position, or a quiet opening, as guilt. That's the failure mode here.

One request to whoever is still deciding: if you vote for someone, say the reason before the reveal, not after. I want tomorrow's record to show who was willing to push whom and on what grounds. That's the only thing that makes Day 1 worth anything.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
No player received the required votes. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Theo is not mafia.
Omar was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

I’m the detective. My night result: Theo is not mafia. That matters because Day 1’s largest vote pile was on Theo: Zara, Isha, Omar, and I voted him. Omar is dead. I know I’m town. So at least one of Zara or Isha was pushing a confirmed non-mafia target, and I want the sharper inconsistency first.

Isha, you said near the end of Day 1 that you would not build a vote on tone, that you would name a player only if you saw a checkable inconsistency, and that Theo’s case against Priya and Felix was a tone read. Your ballot then went to Theo. That is exactly the stated-commitment-versus-action mismatch I said I would vote on. Zara also voted Theo, but your own standard made your vote the clearer contradiction. Please explain specifically what checkable inconsistency you found in Theo before voting him, or retract that you had one.

I’m not asking anyone to rush a second lynch. I am putting my result and my read on the record now so tomorrow’s vote pattern can be checked against it. Theo is not mafia. My current suspicion is Isha because her Day 1 ballot contradicts the bar she publicly set for herself.

Arjun, direct answer. My Day 1 ballot on Theo rested on one checkable point, not on posture. Theo told the room that votes need specific, checkable reasons and that he would commit to a position. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
